slides.title: Welcome to the Nagarika Club!
slides.tip: Play welcome music. Confirm everyone is seated in groups.

slides.title: Introduction
kn_script: Hello everyone! Welcome back to the Nagarika Club!
Last session, we explored the amazing diversity of India through our quiz on states, dances, food and landmarks.
Today, let's think about something interesting — what does culture mean to you?
When I say the word 'culture', what comes to your mind? Is it food? Festivals? Clothes? Language? Music?
Let's hear from a few of you!
slides.tip: Play MC video. Let 3-4 students share what culture means to them.

slides.title: Recall — Last Session
body: In the last session, we explored India's diversity through a fun quiz on states, dances, food and landmarks.
Today we will explore how our cultures mix and create something new and beautiful!
slides.tip: Quick recap of Session 7. Keep this brief — move to new content.

slides.title: What is Composite Culture?
body: Composite Culture means a culture that is made up of many different influences blended together.
India's composite culture comes from centuries of different communities, religions, and traditions living together and sharing their customs.
Our food, music, clothing, festivals, and even our languages show this beautiful mixing!
slides.tip: Explain composite culture with everyday examples students can relate to.

slides.title: Examples of Composite Culture
body: Biryani — a dish with Persian and Indian origins, now loved across all of India!
Bollywood songs — blend Hindi, Urdu, Punjabi, and even English words.
Clothing like the Salwar Kameez — worn across religions and regions.
Festivals — Diwali, Eid, Christmas, Pongal — celebrated together in many neighbourhoods.
slides.tip: Ask students: 'Can you think of more examples from your own life?'

slides.title: Desi or Videsi? — Quiz Time!
body: We will now play a fun game called 'Desi or Videsi?'
I will show you something — food, clothing, sport, or an item.
You have to guess: Is it originally from India (Desi) or did it come from outside (Videsi)?
Ready? Let's find out!
slides.tip: Build excitement for the quiz. Explain the Desi vs Videsi concept clearly.

slides.title: Desi or Videsi? — Question 1

items.label: Samosa — Desi or Videsi?
items.detail: Videsi! The samosa originated in the Middle East (called 'sambosa'). It came to India through Central Asian traders and merchants.

slides.tip: Let students vote by raising hands before revealing the answer.

slides.title: Desi or Videsi? — Question 2

items.label: Chess — Desi or Videsi?
items.detail: Desi! Chess originated in India as 'Chaturanga' during the Gupta Empire (around 6th century). It spread to Persia and then to the world.

slides.tip: Most students will be surprised! Chess is one of India's great gifts to the world.

slides.title: Desi or Videsi? — Question 3

items.label: Jalebi — Desi or Videsi?
items.detail: Videsi! Jalebi came from the Middle East (called 'Zulabiya'). It was brought to India by Turkish and Persian traders.

slides.tip: Another surprise for students!

slides.title: Desi or Videsi? — Question 4

items.label: Yoga — Desi or Videsi?
items.detail: Desi! Yoga is an ancient Indian practice with roots going back over 5,000 years. It is now practiced worldwide!

slides.tip: Celebrate India's contribution to global wellness.

slides.title: Desi or Videsi? — Question 5

items.label: Tea (Chai) — Desi or Videsi?
items.detail: Videsi! Tea originally came from China. The British introduced large-scale tea cultivation in India (Assam, Darjeeling). But chai as we know it — with milk, sugar, and spices — that's our Desi twist!

slides.tip: Great example of composite culture — foreign origin, Indian innovation!

slides.title: Desi or Videsi? — Question 6

items.label: Zero (the number) — Desi or Videsi?
items.detail: Desi! The concept of zero as a number was developed in India by the mathematician Aryabhata. It revolutionised mathematics worldwide!

slides.tip: India's contribution to world knowledge. Celebrate this with students!

slides.title: What Did We Learn?
body: Many things we think of as 'Indian' actually came from other cultures — and many Indian innovations went out to the world!
This is the beauty of composite culture — sharing, mixing, and creating something new together.
No culture is 'pure' — all cultures grow by learning from each other.
slides.tip: Reinforce the key learning: cultures are always mixing and evolving.

slides.title: Composite Culture in Your Life
body: Think about your own daily life:
The clothes you wear — who influenced them?
The food you eat — where did the recipes come from?
The words you use — how many languages do you mix?
The festivals you celebrate — do you celebrate festivals from other communities too?
slides.tip: Make it personal. Ask individual students to share examples from their own lives.

slides.title: Why Does Composite Culture Matter?
body: It teaches us that no one culture has all the answers.
It shows us that sharing makes everyone richer.
It reminds us that India's strength comes from its diversity.
It helps us respect and appreciate people who are different from us.
slides.tip: Connect this to constitutional values — unity in diversity.

slides.title: Group Discussion
body: Share one example of composite culture from your family or neighbourhood.
Why do you think it is important to learn about and respect other cultures?
How can we celebrate diversity in our school?
slides.tip: Give groups 3-4 minutes to discuss, then share with the class.

slides.title: Reflection
kn_script: Wasn't that amazing? We discovered so many surprising things today!
Who knew that our favourite samosa and jalebi came from faraway lands?
And who knew that chess and yoga — two things the whole world loves — started right here in India?
This is what makes our culture so special — we welcome, we share, we grow together.
Remember: respecting other cultures doesn't make your culture less — it makes all of us more!
slides.tip: Play MC video. Let the message sink in — this is the emotional takeaway.

slides.title: Start, Stop, Continue
questions: What's one new thing you want to START doing to appreciate other cultures?
What's one thing you want to STOP doing that shows disrespect to any culture?
What's one thing you want to CONTINUE doing that celebrates diversity?
slides.tip: Encourage different children to share their thoughts for each question.

slides.title: Ripple Tasks
body: Ask your parents or grandparents about a food, word, or tradition in your family that came from another culture.
Learn to say 'Hello' and 'Thank You' in two languages you don't speak.
slides.tip: Assign ripple tasks as take-home activities.

slides.title: Constitution Connect
body: The Preamble of the Indian Constitution talks about FRATERNITY — a sense of brotherhood and sisterhood among all people.
Composite culture is fraternity in action — when we share, learn from, and celebrate each other's cultures, we build brotherhood.
slides.tip: Connect today's learning to the Constitution.

slides.title: Constitution Connect Question
slides.question: How can the values of equality and justice in the Constitution's Preamble be applied in daily life? Can you guess the correct option?
options: By treating everyone with respect, starting with your family and friends
By being mindful of how you and those around you behave towards one another
By speaking out against discrimination and standing up for others' rights
slides.tip: This is a trick question — all options are correct! Reveal with excitement.

slides.title: Together for Change Project
body: Teacher to distribute the 'Diversity & Composite Culture' project card to each group.
You have 3 weeks to complete the activities given in the project card.
Please follow the instructions provided in the project cards thoroughly in your groups.
Consult the teacher if you have doubts!
slides.tip: Distribute project cards. Explain the timeline and expectations clearly.
